memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: "These are the amounts of the materials used for the tabernacle, the tabernacle of the covenant law, which were recorded at Moses' command by the Levites under the direction of Ithamar son of Aaron, the priest." - Exod 38:21 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
An audit. Moses ordered a full public accounting of every material given.

Think about why. Moses was Israel's undisputed leader, who spoke with God face to face. Nobody was demanding receipts. He could easily have said that his integrity should be assumed.

Instead he had it all recorded, by named people, under named supervision.

This is a model worth taking seriously. Paul did the same thing with the collection for Jerusalem, deliberately sending several men so that no one could criticise the way he administered it — taking pains to do what is right not only in the eyes of the Lord but also in the eyes of man (2 Cor 8:20-21).

Integrity is not only about being honest. It is about being visibly, checkably honest, so that trust is protected.

This applies well beyond church finances. Household money. Business expenses. Time we claim to have worked. Reporting to those we answer to. Christians should be the easiest people in the world to audit.

Notice also that Ithamar was Aaron's son — from the family that had failed badly at the golden calf. God restored that family into positions of trust and responsibility.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. Would your handling of money and time survive an audit?
2. Where might you need to be more transparent, even though no one has asked?
3. Do you protect other people's trust as carefully as your own reputation?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Lord, make me trustworthy in what I handle, and transparent even when no one is checking. Amen.
